nodes.content: Learn reduced models of partially observed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics preserving stationary energy distributions and responses to unseen forcing.
requirements: Stationary energy-distribution Wasserstein-1 error stays below 5% of the full-system distribution’s standard deviation.
Predict nonzero mean-energy responses to unseen weak forcing within 10% relative error against full-system simulations.

nodes.content: Fit a history-encoded stochastic latent SDE conditioned on forcing projections, regularized by energy-distribution Wasserstein loss and weak-force response kernels.
Are 16 observation snapshots sufficient for the latent SDE to capture hidden-mode memory driving mean-energy responses?
Sixteen snapshots at 0.25-time-unit spacing capture hidden-mode memory, yielding <10% relative mean-energy response error under held-out weak forcing.
Train matched latent SDEs using 4, 16, or 64 snapshots; compare held-out forcing response errors and stationary-energy Wasserstein distances.
Fit 4/16/64-snapshot latent SDEs on eight observed KS Fourier modes; measure normalized energy W1 and held-out forcing-response errors.
KS-MemoryBench v1 contains 4/16/64-snapshot SDE checkpoints, held-out forcing trajectories, and normalized energy-W1 and mean-response error tables.
Audit KS-MemoryBench v1: compare 4/16/64-snapshot held-out response errors against 10% and normalized energy W1 against 0.05.
KS-MemoryBench v1: 16 snapshots achieved 7.8% held-out response error and 0.039 normalized energy W1; four snapshots yielded 15.1%.
Stratify KS-MemoryBench v1 held-out forcing trajectories by spatial mode and sign; bootstrap 16-snapshot mean-energy response errors.
Mode-3 negative forcing yielded 18.2% mean-energy response error (95% bootstrap CI 13.4–23.1%) despite 7.8% pooled error.
Does the mode-3 negative-forcing error reflect inadequate sign-resolved response training rather than insufficient 16-snapshot memory?
Sixteen snapshots suffice with sign-resolved response regularization, rather than longer histories, to reduce held-out mode-3 negative-forcing error below 10%.
Train 16/64-snapshot SDEs with or without sign-resolved response losses on separate perturbations; compare held-out mode-3 negative-forcing errors.
Using KS-MemoryBench v1 splits, retrain 16/64-snapshot SDEs with/without sign-resolved loss; measure held-out mode-3 negative-forcing response errors.
With sign-resolved loss, held-out mode-3 negative-forcing error was 12.6% at 16 snapshots versus 8.1% at 64.
Estimate conditional mutual information between 4–16-unit-old observations and held-out mode-3 negative-forcing energy responses, given 16 recent KS-MemoryBench v1 snapshots.
For mode-3 negative forcing, older observations added 0.006 bits of conditional information, versus 0.11 bits from recent snapshots.
Does the 64-snapshot model improve mode-3 forcing responses by denoising observations rather than exploiting longer memory?
A noise-aware 16-snapshot encoder will match 64-snapshot mode-3 response accuracy (<10%), implying extra frames primarily improve denoising.
With matched sign-resolved losses, compare noise-aware 16-snapshot and baseline 64-snapshot encoders on clean/noisy held-out mode-3 responses.
Using KS-MemoryBench v1, train a noise-aware 16-snapshot encoder with sign-resolved loss; compare mode-3 response errors against 64-snapshot baselines.
Noise-aware 16-snapshot encoding reduced held-out mode-3 negative-forcing error to 8.4% from 12.6%; the 64-snapshot baseline achieved 8.1%.
Inject 0%, 5%, and 10% observation noise into KS-MemoryBench v1; compare matched-loss 16/64-snapshot mode-3 response errors.
At 10% observation noise, noise-aware 16-snapshot mode-3 response error rose to 14.3%, versus 8.7% for 64 snapshots.
On KS-MemoryBench v1, restore clean observations after 10% noise injection and compare 16/64-snapshot mode-3 response errors.
With clean observations restored, mode-3 negative-forcing error was 8.4% for noise-aware 16 snapshots versus 8.1% for 64.
Use noise-aware 16-snapshot encoders for clean data, switching to 64 snapshots at 10% observation noise to retain sub-10% responses.
Build a Mori–Zwanzig reduced model for observed Fourier modes with learned memory, energy-matched colored noise, and forcing-affine drift.
Can a forcing-independent memory kernel reproduce unseen mode-3 negative-forcing responses while preserving the stationary energy distribution?
Fit matched fixed-kernel and forcing-conditioned Mori–Zwanzig models; compare stationary energy W1 and held-out mode-3 negative-forcing response errors.
Fit fixed and forcing-conditioned memory kernels on KS-MemoryBench v1 training splits; evaluate held-out mode-3 response error and normalized energy W1.
MZ-KS v1 contains fixed/forcing-conditioned kernel checkpoints and held-out mode-3 response-error and normalized energy-W1 tables.
Audit MZ-KS v1 checkpoints against 0.05 normalized energy-W1 and 10% held-out response thresholds, including mode-3 negative forcing.
MZ-KS v1 fixed/conditioned kernels achieved energy W1 of 0.043/0.041, but held-out mode-3 response errors were 17.6%/12.8%.
Defer MZ-KS v1: both kernels match stationary energy, but 12.8% best mode-3 response error exceeds the 10% target.
Learn a history-aware, energy-stratified Markov operator with forcing-controlled transitions, calibrated to stationary energy distributions and response susceptibilities.
Do 32 history-conditioned energy strata resolve mode-3 negative-forcing susceptibility without introducing sparse-transition bias?
A 32-stratum operator with shrinkage-smoothed transitions achieves <0.05 normalized energy W1 and <10% held-out mode-3 response error.
Fit history-conditioned, forcing-controlled 32-stratum operators with shrinkage; measure held-out mode-3 response error, normalized energy W1, and transition sparsity.
The 32-stratum operator achieved 0.037 normalized energy W1 and 8.9% held-out mode-3 response error, versus 12.8% for MZ-KS.
Bootstrap rare-stratum transitions; compare smoothed versus unsmoothed 32-stratum operators on held-out mode-3 response error and normalized energy W1.
Rare-transition bootstraps raised smoothed operators’ overall held-out mode-3 response error from 8.9% to 11.3% median (unsmoothed: 15.0%).
Can pooling neighboring energy strata stabilize rare transitions without erasing mode-3 negative-forcing susceptibility?
Pooling adjacent sparse strata preserves mode-3 susceptibility while keeping bootstrapped response error below 10% and normalized energy W1 below 0.05.
Pool adjacent strata with fewer than 100 training transitions; bootstrap held-out mode-3 response errors and normalized energy W1.
Merge adjacent strata below 100 transitions in the 32-stratum operator; run 500 bootstraps of mode-3 response error and energy W1.
Pooled strata yielded 9.2% median bootstrapped mode-3 response error (95th percentile 9.8%) and 0.042 normalized energy W1.
Adopt pooled-stratum operator: pooling reverses bootstrap degradation (11.3% to 9.2% median response error) while retaining 0.042 normalized energy W1.
Fit a forcing-affine stochastic Koopman generator on delay coordinates, calibrating its invariant energy law and mode-specific linear susceptibilities.
Can a 16-delay Koopman generator infer unseen negative mode-3 susceptibility from positive-forcing data without sacrificing invariant energy accuracy?
Fit 16-delay Koopman generators on unforced and positive mode-3 trajectories; test unseen negative responses and normalized stationary-energy W1.
Train forcing-affine 16-delay Koopman generators on unforced/positive mode-3 KS trajectories; evaluate negative-forcing response error and energy W1.
Koopman-KS v1 contains 16-delay generator checkpoints, negative-mode-3 response predictions, and normalized stationary-energy W1 scores.
Audit Koopman-KS v1: compare unseen negative-mode-3 response error with 10% and normalized invariant-energy W1 with 0.05.
Koopman-KS v1 attained 0.034 normalized energy W1 and 9.1% unseen negative-mode-3 response error.
Using Koopman-KS v1, sweep held-out negative mode-3 forcing amplitudes 0.01–0.05 and measure relative mean-energy response errors.
Across forcing amplitudes 0.01–0.05, Koopman-KS v1 predicted nonzero mean-energy responses with 7.8–9.7% relative error.
Does Koopman-KS v1 retain sub-10% mean-energy response error for unseen time-varying negative mode-3 forcing?
Koopman-KS v1 predicts nonzero mean-energy shifts under unseen sinusoidal mode-3 forcing with <10% relative error up to frequency 0.2.
Simulate held-out negative mode-3 sinusoidal forcing at frequencies 0.05–0.2; compare Koopman-KS mean-energy shifts with full KS.
Simulate Koopman-KS v1 and full KS under unseen mode-3 forcing −0.03+0.01sin(ωt), ω=0.05–0.2; compare mean-energy shifts.
Sinusoidal mean-energy shift errors stayed at 8.0–9.6%, but unforced-control stationary energy W1 reached 0.061 on longer rollouts.
Extend Koopman-KS v1 sinusoidal and unforced-control rollouts to 10,000 time units; track energy W1 and mean-response error by horizon.
At 10,000 time units, Koopman-KS unforced energy W1 rose to 0.074, while sinusoidal mean-response error remained 9.4%.
Retain Koopman-KS for response prediction, but defer adoption: long-horizon energy W1 reaches 0.074 despite sub-10% forcing errors.
